newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-WEST HAM HAVE TOO MANY FOREIGN PLAYERS, SAYS BILIC.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WEST HAM HAVE TOO MANY FOREIGN PLAYERS, SAYS BILIC.

text.p: Croatian international defender Slaven Bilic says West Ham United's premier league position is "frightening" and thinks the club has too many foreign players.
West Ham sit third from the bottom following an uninspired performance last Monday which saw them lose 2-0 to goal-shy Leeds United in front of an increasingly angry home crowd.

On Saturday, things got even worse as the club suffered a humiliating home defeat, this time at the hands of second division giant-killers Wrexham, ending their English Football Association Cup (F.A.) hopes in a third round replay with a goal in the 90th minute.
Manager Harry Redknapp said afterwards he would resign if the chairman wanted him to. The board, traditionally supportive of its manager, has yet to make a decision.

The supporters, who had clearly lost patience with West Ham's appalling record -- one win in 15 matches, and only one goal scored in the last five -- flooded the pitch at the end of the game and united in a chorus of "sack the board".
Fans plan to distribute 15,000 red cards among the crowd at next Wednesday's game against title contenders Arsenal in a bid to reinforce their protest.
Redknapp has faced criticism as his controversial strategy of buying foreign players over local talent has yet to pay dividends.
At one point this season West Ham had 11 overseas players on their books, more than any other club in the country, with eight playing for the first team, but the influx has failed to bring success.

Portuguese striker Paolo Futre arrived last July only to quit in November with a knee injury while Romanian internationals Ilie Dumitrescu and Florin Raducioiu showed only brief flashes of form and failed to slot effectively into the club.
Bilic, 28, said of the two Romanians, "They didn't settle in...I don't know who is to blame." In a veiled criticism he added:: "If you are a good player you have to be capable of playing anywhere."
Dumitrescu has since been sold to Mexican club America Ciudad while Raducioiu - a star of the 1994 World Cup - has failed to hold down a first team place.
The failure of Redknapp's foreign gamble has left West Ham with a lame attacking force underlined by the fact that the club's top scorer with five goals this season is Julian Dicks, a defender.

West Ham have a strong tradition of fostering local talent from East London so Redknapp's strategy has proved controversial. Bilic said the change was due to budget limitations and the influence of big business in the game.
"We [foreign players] were cheaper and he thought us better," Bilic said. Redknapp has always argued that his limited budget went much further abroad.

Although Bilic supports the principle of bringing in players he considers "bigger stars," he said: "The nucleus should be from England and we should build with foreigners...My personal view is that there are too many of us."

Strangely enough, Saturday's game saw Redknapp revert to type, playing Frank Lampard and Rio Ferdinand, both local talents. They turned in good performances creating plenty of chances, albeit wasted ones.
To add to the fans' frustration, the club's board continues to deliberate on accepting an offer of eight million pounds ($13 million) from multimillionaire investor Michael Tabor.

Bilic likened the state of English soccer to that of the Italian game 10 years ago when the lure of big money contracts and the prestige of playing in what was perceived as the world's best league resulted in a huge influx of foreign players.
He had this to say about English soccer today: "It is much quicker than Italian which is better tactically but the same technically. In England there is much less space, you have to move quickly."
Bilic, nicknamed "Super-Slav" by his teammates, arrived at Upton Park in January last year and has proved a great asset to the club.

His talents shone through last Monday's game when he rattled the Leeds crossbar with a ferocious shot from just outside the area. While being a pillar of strength in defence, Bilic is prone to fruitful strikes into the opposing half and his height has made him a force to be reckoned with in the air.
"I have settled down really well," he said. "I am enjoying it very much."
Bilic, who is a law graduate, had wanted to come and play in London ever since he had visited while representing his home team Hadjuk Split against Tottenham in the 1991 UEFA Cup.

He said he had been welcomed by the fans, and added that the feeling was mutual. "They are very passionate," he said, and added that he enjoyed the family atmosphere at the club, something he had not encountered in his European experience. But the club's current league position was "frightening."

West Ham will have a tough match on Wednesday against third placed Arsenal, and Bilic will face the lethal goalscoring combination of Dutch international Dennis Bergkamp and Ian Wright who leads the league goalscoring chart on 23.
Bilic, while stressing his utmost respect for the duo, said: "I can't say I will stop them but I am not afraid of any striker in this world."
